paras: Every studio hands you a document on your first day, and almost nothing that matters is in it. The printed rules are the easy ones. You must wear the pass. You must not bring food into the control room. Equipment in studio two is off limits after eleven. Those are real, and somebody wrote them because something once went wrong, but you can read them in four minutes and then forget them, because the room enforces them for you.

The rules that decide whether you are invited back are the unwritten ones, and nobody will ever tell you what they are. You should not cut in while somebody is listening back to a take, even if you are right, and especially if you are right. If you spot a problem you should flag it early, in one sentence, and not save it for the moment it becomes expensive. If you are going to be late you have to send a heads-up before you are late, not after, because the second one is not information, it is an apology. And if you build a workaround, you must tell somebody, because a workaround that only one person understands is a bomb with a long fuse.

It helps to know which kind of rule you are dealing with, and English makes that distinction out loud. Must and must not usually come from inside the building: the studio decided. Have to often comes from outside it: the union contract, the broadcaster, the client. Should is advice, and it is the form the unwritten rules come in, which is exactly why they are easy to ignore. Can and may are about permission, and the difference between them is mostly how formal the room is.

One last thing, and it is the rule that people learn slowest. Overtime and being on call are not the same thing, and neither of them is the same as goodwill. A deadline that is mandatory should be treated as mandatory, and a deadline that is really a preference should be renegotiated in daylight, in advance, and in writing. Everybody in this industry has stayed until four in the morning for a deadline that turned out to be a preference. It only has to happen twice before you start asking which kind it is.

choices: To list the official safety rules of a recording studio.
To show that the rules that matter are unwritten, and that English marks where each rule comes from.
To argue that studios should stop asking people to work overtime.

tips: You must wear the pass in the building.
Must for a rule from inside: the studio decided it.

items.situation: Now state a rule that comes from outside the building.
tips: We have to deliver by Friday, because the broadcaster set the date.
Have to when somebody else set the rule and you are only passing it on.

items.situation: Give advice to somebody new in the room, twice: once positive, once negative.
tips: You should flag a problem early. You should not cut in while somebody is listening back.
Should is advice, and it is where the unwritten rules live.

items.situation: Say that something is forbidden, and then say that something is simply not necessary.
tips: You must not bring food into the control room. You do not have to stay tonight.
Must not is prohibition. Do not have to is the absence of obligation. They are opposites.

items.situation: Ask for permission in two registers: to a colleague, and to a client.
tips: Can I use studio two after eleven? May I take five minutes of your time?
Can is normal. May is the formal room.

listenings.text: On your first day somebody will hand you two pages of rules, and I want to be honest with you about them. Read them, follow them, and then understand that they are not what anyone will judge you on. Nobody has ever been asked to leave a studio for forgetting a lanyard. People are asked to leave for three other things, and none of them are printed anywhere. The first is talking during playback. The second is discovering a problem at nine in the morning and mentioning it at six in the evening, when it costs four times as much to solve. And the third, which is the one that surprises people, is being right in the wrong tone of voice. You can be the most technically correct person in the room and still be the reason the session slowed down. So here is the only rule I would put on the wall: if you have to choose between being right and being useful, be useful first, and be right about thirty seconds later.

I want to talk about the word deadline, because in this industry it means two completely different things and nobody separates them out loud. There are dates that exist because of physics or because of a contract. The show goes out on Sunday at nine. The broadcaster has the slot. Nothing you do on Saturday night changes that, and if you miss it there is no show. That is a real deadline, and you must treat it as one. And then there are dates that exist because somebody wanted a comfortable margin, which is a perfectly reasonable thing to want, but it is not the same thing at all. I spent the first four years of my career treating both kinds identically, and I stayed until four in the morning more times than I want to count for dates that moved the following week without anybody telling me. So now I ask one question, early, and in a friendly voice: is this date fixed, or is this date a preference? Nobody has ever been offended by that question. Several people have been embarrassed by it, which is a different thing, and usually useful.

extra_audio.text: Pedro explains that the printed rules are the easy ones: you must wear the pass and you must not bring food into the control room. He says the rules that matter are unwritten, and that nobody tells you what they are. He gives the first one: you should not cut in while somebody is listening back to a take. He gives the second one: you should flag a problem early, in one sentence. He adds that if you are going to be late you have to send a heads-up before you are late, not after. Then he asks the other person what the unwritten rules are where they work.
